## Loading necessary libraries for this assignment:

```{r libraries}

library(tidyverse) # For piping and ggplot
```

## Problem 1: Birthday Probability

For this problem, we are writing a function that, given a fixed number of people, _n_, we can obtain the probability that at least two of those people share a birthday. Note that we are assuming a uniform distribution of birthday across the 365 days of the year, and we do not consider leap years.

Instead of directly calculating the probability, we can make use of a simulation for a group of _n_ people where we randomly assign them a birthday. In this case, instead of directly using dates, we can just use the range 1:365 corresponding to the days of the year. For this we need to also double check that our sampling allows for repeats, since we are checking for the probability of duplicate birthdays. This is done with the 'replace' parameter (see code below).

It is important to note that our old and reliable _rnorm()_ function does not work for this problem since we are not getting values from a normal distribution, so I looked online at examples of how to take random samples and saw the use of the _sample()_ function here:

https://pubs.wsb.wisc.edu/academics/analytics-using-r-2019/draw-a-random-sample.html

From here we can write a function that helps us determine the birthday duplicates, so we write a function that takes the parameter value of 'n' birthdays and then calculates the probability of appearing more than once. I found a useful post on Stack o¿Overflow to check for this and grabbed inspiration for my code:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71083995/identifying-duplicates-in-a-list-of-character-vectors-in-r

To summarize: the function takes the fixed group size, then randomly generates a day out of 365 for each person, checks for duplication, returns Boolean value:

```{r any_duplicates}

# Taking my 'n' parameter, corresponding to the fixed amount of people in the room:

birthday_dupl = function(n) {
  
  # We first and foremost need to ensure the value entered is numeric,
  # so we can do a similar check as the one we covered during our Writing Functions lecture:
  
   if (!is.numeric(n)) {
    stop("Input must be numeric. Try again.")
   }
  
  # Now, we need to create a random sample for the birthdays given the range of the year.
  # We can use 'sample()' per the blog post I found using the range of 1-365 corresponding to the days of the year,
  # Moreover, we need to make sure we use 'replace = TRUE' in order to allow for potential duplicates:
  
  birth_sample = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  
  # Based on the StackOverflow article above, I can use the 'duplicated()' function to check for any duplicated values.
  # Per the post, using 'any()' will return a Boolean TRUE or FALSE value:
  
  any_dupl = any(duplicated(birth_sample))
  
  # We can now just simply ask to return this Boolean:
  
  any_dupl
  
}


# Testing my function:

birthday_dupl(500)

```

Voila! We have created the function to check if there are duplicate birthdays in the fixed group. Now, to check for the actual probability, we can use a similar approach like the one we covered in the _Simulation_ lecture, where we used the _expand_grid()_ function to run the 10,000 iterations specified in the assignment instructions. This will be done for groups of sizes between 2-50 people, and we can then use the function we just created above on each:

```{r thousands_times}

# Just like we did in lecture, we need to set the seed to make sure we are getting the same results:

set.seed(1)

# Using 'expand_grid()' just like we did for the Simulation lecture:

sim_bd = 
  expand_grid(
    group = 2:50, # Using the range provided in the instructions
    iter = 1:10000
  ) %>% 
  
  #For this I first tried using the 'map()' function we covered in lecture, but my plot was not working.
  #Then I did a quick Google search and saw that, for Boolean/logical values, I actually need to use the 'map_lgl()' function:
  
  mutate(
    dupl_map = map_lgl(group, birthday_dupl) #Using same approach to mapping as in lecture
  )

# Let's examine:

head(sim_bd, 5)

```

Now, from here, I can calculate the probability for each of the groups. Luckily, the simulation above created a data frame where each row is an iteration for a particular group size. Since we used the duplication assessor function earlier, our simulation returns Boolean values to denote if there is a duplicate or not. We can thus group by our group sizes and just take the mean of the Boolean values across the iterations to get our probability:

```{r probability_plot}

# Creating the data frame with grouped by group size:

birthday_groups = 
  sim_bd %>% # Using the data frame from the simulation we just ran
  group_by(group) %>% # Grouping by group sizes
  summarize(
    bd_prob = mean(dupl_map) #Obtaining the probability simply by getting the mean of the Boolean values
  )

# We can now create the plot of the probability distribution using our old and reliable 'ggplot':

birthday_groups %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = bd_prob)) + 
  geom_line() + # Showing trend line
  geom_point() + # Putting all our points in scatter plot form
  theme_minimal() + #Using this like I did in Homework 4
  labs(
    title = "Probability Distribution of At Least Two People\nSharing a Birthday in a Random Sample",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Two Birthdays Shared"
  )

```
**Plot Description:** As we can see from the plot above, the probability that two people in the same room share the same birthday increases as the group size (n) increases. It is important to note that the increase is non-linear, and follows a somewhat sigmoidal shape. In the case of very small groups, the probability is close to zero, and then increases fast once the group size reaches around n = 10. We can see that the probability is about 50% around when n = 25, and it becomes very close to 100% once you reach 50 people. 

## Problem 2: Analyzing Longitudinal Study Data

### Using Iteration to Load Our Data

For this problem, we can use a very similar approach like the one used in the _Iterations and List Columns_. Just as the hint provided states, we can make use of the _list.files()_ function in order to read all of our files at once, for both the experimental and the control arms of the study.

Then, on the same pipe, I am also making use of the _purrr::map_ function, as hinted by the instructions, to iterate through each of the names and be able to load our data at once:

```{r reading_files}

# Using a very similar approach as the one covered in lecture.

# Saving my result as a new variable per the instructions, and using the 'purrr'
# package with the 'map' function:

full_long_names = 
  tibble(
    files = list.files("./HW5_Data/"),
    path = str_c("./HW5_Data/", files)
  ) %>%
  mutate(data = purrr::map(path, read_csv)
         ) %>% 
  unnest(data)

# Inspecting the data frame:

head(full_long_names, 5)

names(full_long_names)

```

### Tidying our Data

Great! Now we can proceed to tidy our data. Following the examples covered in the _Iteration and List Columns_, we notice that some important variables are contained within others, such as the name, which includes the type of study group (i.e., control or experiment), and the subject ID number.

Moreover, we see that our data is panel data, or in other words, it is in wide format. Thus, we can use our old and reliable _pivot_longer()_ function to grab all weekly observations and put them in long format, and that way, our tidy data frame should contain the study group, the week, the subject ID, and what the outcome was.

```{r tidying_long}

# Creating a new tidy data frame for my longitudinal data:

tidy_long_df =
  full_long_names %>% 
  # We can clean variable names just like we have done in previous asssignments using the janitor package:
  janitor::clean_names() %>% 
  
  # From here, we can use a similar approach as the one done in lecture and make use of the 'str_replace'
  # function to remove the '.csv' name from the files column in our data frame:
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3) # Grabbing only the first three characters of name
  ) %>% 
  
  # Now we need to change our data from the 'wide' format to 'long' format using our well-known
  # 'pivot_longer()' function:
  
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8, # Grabbing the number of weeks included in the df
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) %>% 
  # Had issues in steps below with the data analysis for the spaghetti chart and it was because weeks 
  # was detected as a string rather than a numeric value, so mutating here:
  
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) %>% 
  
  # We can now use 'select()' in order to keep the variables we need
  # for this assignment:
  
  select(group, subject = files, week, outcome)
  
# Visualizing the tidy data frame:

head(tidy_long_df, 5)

```

### Plotting Subjects Over Time

Now that we have our data tidied, we can proceed to create an _speguetti_ plot (using ggplot), which is simply a plot to visualize outcomes across time where each line represents a different participant. We will make use of _geom_path()_ to connect observations for the same subject. This, combined with study branch, will allow us to look at differences for each individual participant and also across study arms. Moreover, I am also using _theme_minimal()_ for better aesthetics, just like I did in the last couple of homeworks.

Since we are looking at the data per study group (i.e., control or experiment), we need to facet by the _group_ variable in our data frame.

```{r spaguetti_plot}

# Creating the spaguetti plot from the tidy data frame created above:

tidy_long_df %>% 
  
  # Making use of case match to make sure my study arms are appropriately labeled.
  # Same process as in previous homeworks:
  
  mutate(
    group = case_match(
      group,
      "con" ~ "Control",
      "exp" ~ "Experiment"
    )
  ) %>% 
  
  # We use the 'subject' variable we created above 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subject, color = subject)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() + 
  facet_grid (. ~ group) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", # Removing the subject legends
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + # Centering the title
  labs(
    title = "Subject Outcome Across Time by Study Branch",
    x = "Week Number",
    y = "Subject Outcome"
  )

```

**Describing the Plot:** As we can see from the trend above, the study subjects in the control arm have highly variable outcomes across the eight weeks of the study duration, with a minimum value of `r min(tidy_long_df$outcome[tidy_long_df$group == "con"], na.rm = TRUE)` and a maximum value of `r max(tidy_long_df$outcome[tidy_long_df$group == "con"], na.rm = TRUE)`. Despite this high variability, there is no clear increasing or decreasing trend in the study outcome during the duration of the study.

On the other hand, the participants in the experimental arm of the study display an increasing trend in the study outcome across the eight weeks of the study. The maximum outcome value in this arm at Week 8 was `r max(tidy_long_df$outcome[tidy_long_df$group == "exp" & tidy_long_df$week == 8], na.rm = TRUE)`, which is `r max(tidy_long_df$outcome[tidy_long_df$group == "exp" & tidy_long_df$week == 8], na.rm = TRUE) -max(tidy_long_df$outcome[tidy_long_df$group == "con" & tidy_long_df$week == 8], na.rm = TRUE)` units difference from the higher value on the control arm at Week 8.

Overall, based on this data, I would say that there is a clear difference in outcomes between both study arms, with the experimental arm showing a clear increasing trend. We then may have preliminary evidence to determine a potential association between the treatment and outcome of interest, but not yet able to determine full causality.


## Problem 3: Analyzing Longitudinal Study Data

### Creating a Function for Simulation 

For this problem, we can use a very similar approach like the ones that we utilized for Problem 1, were we create a function to run a t-test given a changeable value for _μ_ and fixed values for both _σ_ and _n_. This is very similar to the example we covered in our _Simulation_ lecture. The main difference compared with Problem 1 is that, in this case, we _do_ make use of our old and reliable _rnorm()_ function:

```{r running_simulation}

# Creating a function to run our simulation, where our input parameter
# will be the value of mu. Note that, per the instructions, we are fixing
# the values for our 'n' to be 30, and our 'sigma' to be 5:

sim_p3 = function(mu_value, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  
  # We can now generate our random sample with our fixed number of observations and sigma:
  
  sim_data = tibble(
     x = rnorm(n, mean = mu_value, sd = sigma),
  )
  
  # Now, per the hint provided, we can just run a t-test to assess the null
  # hypothesis that the true mu = 0.
  
  # Notice that for the t-test we are not using the whole tibble but just the
  # x value we created above for the simulation data:
    
  t_test = t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) %>% 
    broom::tidy()  # Cleaning our results, per assignment hint
  
# Now, per the assignment instructions, we are also asked to keep the sample mu and p-value.
# Recall we obtained the estimate and the p-value from the broom::tidy step above:
    
  t_test %>% 
    select(sample_mu = estimate, p_value = p.value)
  
}

# Let's now test our function with μ = 0:

set.seed(1) # Setting seed so results are reproducible

sim_p3(0)

```

### Creating a Data Frame from Multiple True μ

We have now created a function utilizing the parameters established, and we can now vary the value μ. Now, per the assignment instructios, we can run 5000 iterations for when μ = 0, and then repeat this procedure for μ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

To do this, we can use a very similar approach to what we did in Problem 1 and following the _Simulation_ lecture notes. We first start with the _expand_grid()_ function, just like above, and we do 5,000 iterations for each value of μ. We then use the _purrr::map_ function again and we can just simply apply the function we just created above to each simulation. We can thus obtain a data frame where we will list the inputted (true) μ, the sample's μ and the p-value:

```{r multiple_mu}

# Setting seed before starting to allow for reproducibility:

set.seed(1)

# Just like in problem 1, we can create a data frame for the results of our
# simulation, for all μ values of interest:

sim_p3_results =
  expand_grid(
    mu_value = 0:6, # The values of μ we want to check
    iter = 1:5000 #Iterating 5000 times
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    estimate_df = map(mu_value, sim_p3) # Using the function we created above
  ) %>% 
  unnest(estimate_df)

# Let's visualize our data frame:

head(sim_p3_results, 5)

# Looking good!

```

### Visualizing Power

Now that we have run the needed simulations, we can make a plot showing the proportion of times the null was rejected against the different true values of μ we included. In this case, let us consider the null hypothesis to be:

H_0: μ = 0, with α = 0.05

First, we need to calculate the proportion of time the null was rejected or, in other words, the power of the test. We can do this by creating a variabel where we check if the saved p_values for each iteration are below our significance level (α = 0.05), which would allow us to reject the null. Then, we can just simply group the results of our simulation (using _group_by()_) by each true value of μ and calculate the mean of the rejection value just created:

```{r reject_null}

# Creating a new logical variable in our simulation data frame:

sim_p3_reject =
  sim_p3_results %>% 
  mutate(
    reject = (p_value < 0.05) # this would yield either TRUE or FALSE
  ) %>% 
  group_by(mu_value) %>% # We can now gorup by our true μ values
  summarize(
    reject_prop = mean(reject)
  )

# We can now just make use of ggplot in order to create our plot:

sim_p3_reject %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu_value, y = reject_prop)) + 
  geom_line(color = "orange") + 
  geom_point(color = "darkorange") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + # Centering the title
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Null Hypothesis Rejection (Power) by True μ Value",
    x = "True μ",
    y = "Power",
  )

```

**Describing the Association:** From the figure above, we can see that there is an undeniable positive association between the effect size (the true value of μ) and power (the proportion of times the null hypothesis gets rejected).

The more that the true population means starts distancing itself from zero, the proportion of null hypothesis being rejected increases. We can see this rellationship is sigmoidal, and about when true μ = 4, the proportion of all rejected null hypothesis becomes extremely close to 1 (100% of samples).

### The Fight Between μ̂ against the True μ

Now, let's create another plot showing the showing the average estimate of μ̂ against the true value of μ. To do this, we can take a similar approach like the one we did above, grouping by the true μ value and then, since we already hae a _sample_mu_ variable, we can simply find the mean of it using _summarize()_. Then, we can just create the plot using ggplot:

```{r muhat_vs_mu}

p3_plot_2 =
  sim_p3_results %>% 
  group_by(mu_value) %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_sample_mu = mean(sample_mu) # getting our average values
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu_value, y = mean_sample_mu)) + 
  geom_line(color = "lightgreen") + 
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + # Centering the title
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated μ-hat vs. True μ Value",
    x = "True μ",
    y = "Average Estimated μ-hat",
  )

# Now let's visualize the plot:

p3_plot_2

```

Now, we can make a second plot following the same process as above, but only for the samples in which we rejected the null. We can thus use an almost identical approach as to how the _sim_p3_reject_ data frame was created above, since this data frame contains a variable assessing if we can reject the null hypothesis:

```{r muhat_vs_mu_reject}

p3_plot_3 =
  sim_p3_results %>% 
  filter(p_value < 0.05) %>%  # keeping only samples where null was rejected
  group_by(mu_value) %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_sample_mu = mean(sample_mu) # getting our averages
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu_value, y = mean_sample_mu)) + 
  geom_line(color = "lightblue") + 
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + # Centering the title
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated μ-hat vs. True μ Value*",
    subtitle = "*Only Samples Where Null Hypothesis Was Rejected",
    x = "True μ",
    y = "Average Estimated μ-hat",
  )

# Now let's visualize the plot:

p3_plot_3

```

To better visualize the contrast between these two plots, let's create an overlayed plot. We can make use of most of the code already written above:

```{r overlayed_plot}

# Using same pipe process as first plot:

df_plot2 =
  sim_p3_results %>% 
  group_by(mu_value) %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_sample_mu = mean(sample_mu) # getting our average values
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    which_plot = "All" # Creating identifying variable
  )

# Using same pipe process as second plot:

df_plot3 = 
  sim_p3_results %>% 
  filter(p_value < 0.05) %>%  # keeping only samples where null was rejected
  group_by(mu_value) %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_sample_mu = mean(sample_mu) # getting our averages
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    which_plot = "Rejected Only" # Creating identifying variable
  )

# Merging my data frames:

df_plot4 =
  bind_rows(df_plot2, df_plot3)

# And now making my overlapped po, again, using same structure as plots above:

p3_plot_4 =
  df_plot4 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu_value, y = mean_sample_mu, color = which_plot)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + # Centering the title
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated μ-hat vs. True μ Value*",
    x = "True μ",
    y = "Average Estimated μ-hat",
    color = "Sample Type"
  )

# Now let's visualize the plot:

p3_plot_4


```

**Plots Description & Question Answer:** 
The sample average of μ-hat across tests for which the null is rejected is only approximately equal to the true value of μ when the true μ is relatively large (μ = {4, 5, 6}). 

As we can see from the three plots above, when considering all the samples, the values for the estimated μ-hat almost perfectly align with the values of the true μ. This result was interesting to me, but I believe it makes sense since, when we average all 5,000 simulated samples, for each value of μ — and just like we saw in our _Simulation_ lecture — the sample mean estimates are expected to be more centered around the true population mean.

Moreover, we can see that when we only take the samples for which we reject the null hypothesis, the average estimated μ-hat deviates from the true μ values, in particular when μ = {1, 2 3}. This also makes sense, and it is actually in agreement with what we observed in our Power vs. μ graph: when we have low power, only samples with extreme estimated  μ-hat values will be able to yield a p-value that is below the 0.05 significance threshold. However, as we increase in our true μ values, power (the proportion of null hypothesis rejects) also increases, and thus a greater proportion of the simulated samples will reject the null hypothesis, making very little distinction between the all samples set.

Per the explanation above, we can see that in both the power vs. true effect and in the average estimated μ vs. true μ graphs, it is around true μ = 4 when we lose distinction between the rejected-only averages and the all-sample averages.
